causal_prompt: Revenue rose 20% after our feature launch. Marketing spend and prices also rose that month, and it was our usual busy season. Can we attribute the increase to the feature? What evidence is most useful next?

causal_answer.answer:
No—the 20% increase is consistent with a feature effect, but it does not identify one. Higher prices, marketing, and seasonal demand could explain some or all of it. You need a comparison estimating what revenue would have been without the feature under the same conditions.

The most useful next evidence is a concurrent randomized holdout: assign eligible customers to feature access or no access, with equivalent pricing and marketing exposure. Measure revenue per assigned customer over a predefined window, including non-users, and report the incremental effect with an uncertainty interval against a minimum commercially meaningful lift. This estimates the feature’s effect under those conditions; it does not automatically attribute the historical 20% to it.

If an experiment is impractical, use an unaffected, comparable customer group or market and compare its before/after change with the exposed group’s. Check similar pre-launch trends, equivalent price and marketing changes, and absence of spillovers or other different shocks; the causal conclusion depends on these assumptions.

Collect launch/exposure dates, customer-level revenue, prices, purchases, conversion, and marketing exposure for both groups, plus enough pre-launch history to assess seasonality. Separate price increases from changes in purchasing volume. A before/after total or a survey of feature users alone cannot establish attribution.
